findings.title: Only `pre-advance` has a defined insertion point and status; `pre-tasks` and `pre-implementation` are unmodeled
findings.description:
The config declares `pre-tasks` (reviewType `slice`) and `pre-implementation` (reviewType `tasks`) at lines 83–84. v1 claims to implement them at line 141. The rest of the design only supports the end-of-slice gate:
- `pending-review` is defined as "tasks complete, review gate configured" (line 106).
- The single new branch sits between Priority 5 and Priority 6 (line 115).
- Gating before task breakdown would have to fire at Priority 4 (`needs-tasks`, `WorkflowNavigator.ts:224`). Gating before implementation would have to fire before Priority 5.
- `SliceStatus.status` has no way to say which transition is pending, so one `pending-review` value can't represent three different gates.
- Priority 5 (`in-implementation`) is derived from "tasks not all checked". A task file with 0/N checked is indistinguishable from half-done work. It's undefined whether a missing `tasks` review blocks mid-implementation.
- Line 141 says "the four slice-level transitions", but `pre-slice-plan` is initiative-level and deferred, so there are three.

The gate needs an explicit model. Either the status carries a `gate` field, or each transition has its own derivation hook. As written, the anticipated "Gate logic" slice can't be built from this document.

findings.title: Recommendation vocabulary is inconsistent and gives consumers no structured routing data
findings.description:
- The overview and principles (lines 20, 42) say the gate returns `pending-review` / `review-failed` recommendations. The envisioned state (lines 118, 124) returns `recommendation: "review"` / `"blocked"`. The status enum and the recommendation string are being conflated.
- In `types.ts:280–289`, `NextAction.recommendation` is free-form prose ("Advance to slice 165: …", "Create task breakdown (Phase 5)"). There is no stable vocabulary today, so line 173's claim that Amoeba depends on one is unverified.
- The reviewType to route to, the artifact path and the verdict exist only inside the `rationale` string. The goal at line 32 is that runners act "without parsing recommendation strings", and the `NextAction` shape can't deliver it.
- Line 173 forbids changing the `NextAction` type. Meeting the goal needs an optional structured field such as `review?: { state, reviewType, artifact, verdict }`, and adding one is a compatible change.
- The `blocked` rationale hardcodes "verdict FAIL" (line 124), which is wrong for UNKNOWN-as-fail, parse failures and "cannot read file".

findings.title: "Lexicographically last filename = most recent" is not true for this naming convention
findings.description: The cited convention is `210-review.code.<slug>.md` (line 131). The only varying part after the index and type is a descriptive slug, not a timestamp. Sorting by slug doesn't give recency. A re-review after fixes with a different slug can sort before the earlier FAIL, and the gate keeps reporting `review-failed`. It could equally pick an old PASS over a newer FAIL, which fails open. The detector's existing `matchFiles` sorts ascending and callers take `[0]` (`documentDetector.ts:34–39, 64`), so the proposed "last" also diverges from sibling detection. Order by a frontmatter date field (`dateUpdated` or `dateCreated`) or by mtime, with a defined tiebreak. Alternatively, require that the newest review of the type wins by a documented, contract-owned field.

findings.title: Failure handling cannot work as described: `deriveSliceStatus` swallows errors, and `parseFrontmatter` hides parse failures
findings.description:
- Lines 98 and 149 require that malformed YAML, an unreadable file or a permission error becomes `UNKNOWN`, with a rationale that "names the parse failure explicitly". `parseFrontmatter` (`frontmatterParser.ts:9–49`) never throws and returns `{found:false, data:{}}` for missing frontmatter, an unclosed `---`, or a read error. It doesn't parse YAML at all, so "malformed YAML" is never detected. The gate can't name a cause. A review file that exists but is unreadable looks the same as one with no verdict.
- `deriveSliceStatus` wraps everything in a bare `catch { return base; }` (`WorkflowNavigator.ts:494–496`), and `base.status` is `'no-active-slice'`. Any exception from new review or config code lands there, and `getNext` then recommends "pick your first slice" (Priority 2). That silently skips the gate and gives a misleading recommendation. This directly contradicts "fail-fast on configuration errors" (line 48) and "must not silently pass".

The new review-evaluation code needs its own error boundary, and the parser needs to return a distinguishable failure reason.

findings.title: The frontmatter parser is flat and string-only, which conflicts with the contract fields the document says to carry
findings.description:
`FrontmatterData` is `{[key]: string}` (`types.ts:41–43`), and the parser treats every line containing `:` as a top-level key.
- If Squadron's `criteria` and `provenance` are nested YAML maps or lists, their child lines such as `  verdict: x` or `  - name: y` become top-level keys. A nested `verdict:` could overwrite the real one.
- `score` (a float, line 100) arrives as a string.
- Lines 46 and 100 say CF "carries" `criteria` and `provenance` as opaque fields and "reads and stores" `score`. `DocumentDetectionResult.review` is a path (`string | null`, like its siblings), and there is no review-result type to hold any of this.
- Because the schema is externally owned (Squadron 300), the document should pin the exact frontmatter shape it relies on (verdict is a top-level scalar, case rules). It should also decide whether to extend the parser or add a YAML-aware reader.

The "stored but unused" score and the opaque carried fields have no consumer. They are dead weight until Squadron 301 exists.

findings.title: The path from config to navigator and checker is unspecified, and the claimed worktree scoping doesn't exist in `ConfigManager`
findings.description:
- `WorkflowNavigator` is constructed with no arguments (`workflowTools.ts:154, 200`), and `getNext(project)` takes only `ProjectData`. `ConsistencyChecker` has no config access either. Config reads currently live in the CLI and MCP surfaces (`check.ts:141`, `workflowTools.ts:263`). The design says both surfaces "inherit it without per-surface work" (line 34), but the navigator and checker need either an injected config or a `ConfigManager` dependency. That is a new dependency from introspection onto config, plus a constructor or signature change that line 167 ("no 160 interfaces change") denies.
- Line 171 says the keys "should be resolvable at worktree scope using the resolution chain 180 introduced". `ConfigManager.get` resolves only project, then user, then default (`ConfigManager.ts:91–130`). Worktree scoping exists for project data (`worktree-overlay.ts`), not config. The cited resolution chain for config isn't there, and this is unplanned scope.
- `ConfigManager.get` re-reads and parses two TOML files per call. Per-gate evaluation on every `getNext` and `getStatus` multiplies this. Load config once per call.

findings.title: Nested `review_gates` collides with `ConfigManager`, and the `validate` hook can't be the enforcement point
findings.description:
- Line 145 defers the nested-versus-flat decision. It is load-bearing and should be settled here.
- `ConfigManager.get` and `set` throw "Unknown config key" for anything not statically in `CONFIG_KEYS`, and each definition is a scalar.
- `workflow.review_gates` is a TOML table of inline tables. The dotted-flat option requires 4×2 statically declared keys, or pattern-matching lookup.
- `validate` and `enum` run only inside `set()` (`ConfigManager.ts:145`). `get()` never validates. A hand-edited `.context-forge.toml` with `threshold = "pas"` is never caught, so line 48's "enforcement point" claim is false for the primary way these overrides will be written.
- The doc doesn't say where read-time validation occurs or how a config error is surfaced given that `NextAction` has no error channel.
- Naming is inconsistent: snake_case keys (`review_enabled`) alongside camelCase `reviewType` and `threshold` inside the gates table.

findings.title: The verdict and policy semantics are internally inconsistent
findings.description:
- `review_unknown_as` values are never enumerated. Line 97 uses `fail`, line 147 uses `"concern"` (singular, while the threshold uses `"concerns"`), and line 106 implies a `pending` option ("verdict is UNKNOWN and `review_unknown_as` treats it as pending"). Line 36 says the default threshold "blocks on FAIL or UNKNOWN", which ignores that `review_unknown_as=concern` makes UNKNOWN pass.
- The threshold ordering is undefined. "`concerns` or lower" (line 95) names no lower value, and `threshold = "fail"` would contradict "`FAIL` — always blocks".
- It's unclear whether UNKNOWN-as-fail yields `pending-review` or `review-failed`. Line 106 and line 107 disagree, and the `review-failed` rationale text assumes a FAIL verdict.
- Verdict case sensitivity (`pass` versus `PASS`) is unspecified.

A truth table of verdict × threshold × unknown_as → status would resolve all of this. The "Gate logic" slice promises such a matrix but the architecture should fix it.

findings.title: The consistency rule will retroactively flag every historical slice when gating is enabled
findings.description: The rule fires for any slice "marked complete in the slice plan" without a review (warning) or with a non-clearing verdict (error, line 137). Every slice completed before `review_enabled = true` has no review artifact. Turning the feature on in an existing project produces one finding per historical slice, and `error` severity can fail `cf check`. That undermines "conservative by default" (line 36). The rule also doesn't say which gate's reviewType it checks (only `pre-advance`, presumably) or which slices it scans. There is no grandfathering mechanism, such as a floor index or "only the active slice".

findings.title: The design is heavier than the motivation needs. Cut per-gate overrides, `review_unknown_as`, and the cosmetic renumbering
findings.description:
The stated problem (lines 18, 24) is that the navigator advances after tasks complete without a review. That needs one gate (`pre-advance`), one reviewType and one threshold. The document adds all of the following:
- A four-entry per-transition override table. It is the source of the nested-config problem above, and three of the four entries (`pre-slice-plan`, `pre-tasks`, `pre-implementation`) have no working design or are deferred.
- A third policy knob, `review_unknown_as`, with an unspecified value set and an interaction matrix that line 147 admits will confuse support. Treating UNKNOWN as `FAIL` covers the conservative default. Add the knob only if someone asks.
- Score parsing and storage with no consumer (line 100) and "opaque" `criteria` and `provenance` carrying.
- A defined `pre-slice-plan` transition whose logic is deferred (lines 139–141). The config schema reserves it, but that is speculative surface.
- Priority renumbering or "convert to named stages" (line 151). The existing code already uses a `Priority 2.5` comment, so a comment-only label for the new branch costs nothing. Restructuring the cascade is scope creep and contradicts "extend, don't replace" (line 44).

Recommended v1 is `review_enabled` plus one threshold plus a single `pre-advance` gate keyed on a scalar `reviewType`. Everything else can wait.

findings.title: The "purely additive" claim understates the `SliceStatus` ripple
findings.description: Line 167 says no 160 interfaces change. Widening the `SliceStatus.status` union (`types.ts:257`) changes a public type. Its consumers include `status.ts:162–163`, which prints the raw value, `buildSummary` (`WorkflowNavigator.ts:542+`), and the `workflow_status` tool description that documents the response shape (`workflowTools.ts:127–129`). A slice that passes the gate and is `complete` stays visible as complete. A gated slice stops being `complete`, so any consumer testing `=== 'complete'` (for example the slice-completion counters) now sees it as incomplete. The doc should list the consumers to update.

findings.title: Nothing ties a review verdict to the state of the work it reviewed
findings.description: "Artifact-first truth" (line 40) means a PASS code review stays valid after later commits, reopened tasks, or a re-completed task list. The gate checks presence and verdict only. This is probably acceptable for v1, but the document should state it as a known limitation. A cheap mitigation is comparing the review's date to the task file's `dateUpdated`.
